From Hotel: 14 min · 6 min → Iglesia de La Merced
1.Iglesia de La Merced
The most elaborately decorated facade in Antigua — yellow and white stucco piled with baroque relief work — fronts a working church whose convent ruins behind it hide a huge Spanish fountain and a rooftop with views over the whole town.

2.Arco de Santa Catalina
A golden-yellow baroque archway built in 1694 so cloistered Santa Catalina nuns could cross the street unseen; its clock was added in the 1830s, and the framed view of Volcán de Agua through the arch is Antigua's signature photograph.

3.La Recolección
The most dramatic ruin in Antigua — a monastery built from 1701 with walls thick enough to resist earthquakes, brought down anyway in 1773 and left as a field of toppled columns and collapsed vaulting inside a quiet park.

4.Cerro de la Cruz
A hilltop cross above the north edge of town frames the single best panorama of Antigua's red-tiled roofs and church domes with Volcán de Agua rising behind them; tourist police patrol the path and viewpoint during daylight hours.

1.Antigua Guatemala Cathedral
A working parish chapel faces the plaza, but step around the side and the earthquake-shattered nave behind it — roofless arches, fallen columns, grass growing through the stone floor — is what earned this ruin its fame.

2.Iglesia de San Francisco
A working Franciscan church holding the tomb of Hermano Pedro de San José Betancur, Central America's first canonized saint, whose small museum of personal relics draws a steady line of local pilgrims behind the sanctuary.

3.Palacio de los Capitanes Generales
The seat of Spanish colonial power across Central America, rebuilt in stone after the 1773 earthquake with the longest colonnaded facade on Parque Central; it now houses the National Museum of Guatemalan Art.

Day 3
From Hotel: 1h 10min → Volcán Pacaya
1.Volcán Pacaya
One of Guatemala's three active volcanoes, erupting almost continuously since 1965; a guided trail climbs through pine forest and hardened lava fields to a black volcanic-ash ridge with views into the smoking crater and, on an active night, glowing rock.

Local Tastes
Pepián
Guatemala's national dish — a thick, toasted-spice stew of chicken, beef or pork simmered with vegetables and tomato, found on nearly every menu in Antigua.
Rincón Típico · La Fonda de la Calle Real
Tamales Colorados
Antigua's own tamale variation — corn masa wrapped in banana leaf, filled with pork and a tomato-achiote paste called recado, with a chili inside.
La Cuevita de los Urquizú
Antigua-Grown Coffee
Antigua Valley coffee is one of Guatemala's protected-origin denominations, grown on volcanic soil in the shadow of Agua, Fuego and Acatenango.
Fat Cat Coffee House · San Pedro Las Huertas farms
Food Delivery
Uber Eats
Foreign number: accepted. — verification is the same SMS system as Uber rides; codes arrive on foreign carriers in Antigua.
Covers most restaurants inside the historic center reliably; coverage thins fast toward the edges of town, and delivery can slow during heavy downpours.
ubereats.com
Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted. — verification SMS arrives on foreign carriers; an existing Uber account from home works without re-registering.
Fixed up-front pricing and no cash or Spanish needed, but cars are noticeably scarcer in Antigua than in Guatemala City — expect a longer wait, especially late at night, and keep tuk-tuk moto-taxis as the cash-only backup for short hops around town.
uber.com
Worth Knowing

A colonial capital the earthquakes never let finish being rebuilt

Antigua was Central America's capital for over two centuries until the 1773 earthquakes drove the government to found Guatemala City instead — which is why the ruins here were never cleared away or restored. Walking past a roofless nave or a fallen archway isn't visiting a museum piece; it's the same view a resident had the week the capital moved.

Cash is still the default. Cards are accepted at hotels and the nicer restaurants, but the small entrance fees at the ruins — Q20 to Q40 — are cash-only at the door, and having a stack of small quetzal bills makes the whole three days smoother.

The historic center sits at roughly 1,530 meters above sea level, so afternoons are warm and mornings and evenings are cool year-round — pack a light layer for the cooler hours.

Every street corner carries a hand-painted tile with its colonial name and a small number — the town's own address system, unchanged since the 1700s, and worth glancing at before assuming a phone's navigation app has the modern name right.
